name: Fermented cod liver oil / butter oil (Weston A. Price)
lead: Fermented cod liver oil combined with high-vitamin butter oil is a supplement pairing associated with the Weston A. Price Foundation, a nutrition advocacy group co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig to promote the research of Canadian dentist Weston A. Price (1870 to 1948).[1] Followers use it as a source of fat-soluble vitamins, aiming for well-formed teeth, jaws and facial structure, and good skin and bone development.

Cod liver oil in general is a long-established supplement containing the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA along with vitamins A and D; it was widely used in the 1800s and 1900s against rickets.[3] Price's 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration described his travels studying traditional diets and argued that processed foods caused deficiencies and disease, with photographs of broad faces and straight teeth in groups eating traditional foods that followers still cite for facial structure.[1]

Reviewers at the time and since have disagreed about his work: a 1940 Journal of the American Medical Association review by C. F. Elzea called his approach more evangelistic than scientific, a Canadian Medical Association Journal review the same year called the book a masterpiece, and in 1981 William T. Jarvis argued in Nutrition Today that it reflected a 'myth of the healthy savage'.[1] No clinical studies of the fermented cod liver oil and butter oil combination were found.

paras: Weston Andrew Valleau Price was a Canadian dentist, born in Newburgh, Ontario, on 6 September 1870 and died on 23 January 1948; he graduated from the University of Michigan dental college in 1893 and practiced in Cleveland, Ohio.[1] He chaired the National Dental Association from 1914 to 1928.[1] He worked on dental furnaces, radiography and X-ray effects on cancer, and for about 25 years studied root-filled teeth, arguing that mouth infections caused systemic disease; his focal infection work helped drive tooth extraction in the 1920s and fell out of favour in the 1930s.[1]

By 1930 his focus had turned to nutrition. His 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration reported fieldwork among communities including the Swiss Lötschental and Native American, Polynesian and Aboriginal groups, with about 15,000 photographs according to Wikipedia, and argued that Western diets and food processing removed nutrients and caused tooth decay and other diseases.[1] Anthropologist Earnest A. Hooton wrote the foreword.[1] The book's pictures of broad faces and straight teeth among groups on traditional foods, set against crowding and narrow arches in modern-diet relatives, are the images believers still circulate in facial-structure discussions.[1][4]

The Weston A. Price Foundation was co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig to disseminate Price's work.[1] A separate body, the Price-Pottenger Nutrition Foundation, was established in 1952 and holds an archive of his materials.[1] The Wikipedia article on Price does not discuss butter oil or cod liver oil specifically.

Cod liver oil is made from the liver of Atlantic cod; about 20 percent of it is omega-3 fatty acids, and USDA data cited by Wikipedia list 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A and 34 micrograms of vitamin D per tablespoon.[3] Northern European folk medicine used it for rheumatism and gout, it became a bottled medicine in the 1800s, and after vitamin D deficiency was linked to rickets in 1920 it was promoted as a vitamin D source, with marketers calling it 'bottled sunshine'.[3]
Wikipedia notes that vitamin A accumulates in the liver and can reach harmful levels (hypervitaminosis A), and that one tablespoon exceeds the adult upper limit for vitamin A.[3]

Fermented cod liver oil (FCLO) and high-vitamin butter oil (HVBO) are marketed to Price followers as traditional-food supplements. Cod liver oil is made from the liver of Atlantic cod and, like other fish oils, contains EPA and DHA, with vitamins A and D; Wikipedia gives about 20 percent omega-3 fatty acids and, per USDA data, roughly 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A and 34 micrograms of vitamin D per tablespoon.[3] Butter oil is a concentrated milk fat, and the 'high-vitamin' version is described by proponents as made from cream of cows eating fast-growing grass.

Followers take the two together because they see them as complementary: the cod liver oil for vitamins A and D and omega-3s, and the butter oil for fat-soluble factors they associate with mineral use in teeth and bone, including vitamin K2.[8] Wikipedia's cod liver oil article describes only the general oil; it does not describe a 'fermented' product.[3]

Northern European folk medicine used cod liver oil on the skin and by mouth for rheumatism and gout, and it became a bottled medicine in the 1800s. Observers in 1820s Germany noted that children given it did not develop rickets, and use spread through the 1860s, continuing for rickets prevention into the 1950s.[3] John Bland-Sutton's 1899 addition of the oil to the diet of London Zoo lion cubs stopped their rickets.[3] Elmer McCollum and Marguerite Davis identified vitamin A in 1914, and in 1922 McCollum separated the anti-rickets factor, naming it vitamin D; marketers then promoted the oil as 'bottled sunshine'.[3]

Processing has also changed: the Möller process, invented in 1850, grinds livers into a slurry, simmers it and skims the oil, and modern methods require purification to reduce oxidised fats and contaminants.[3] Wikipedia also records Newfoundland use of the oil as a base for red ochre paint, a historical sidelight with no relation to supplements.[3]

The Weston A. Price Foundation (WAPF) was co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon (Morell) and nutritionist Mary G. Enig; it is a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit and reported about 13,000 members in 2010.[7] Its stated mission is restoring nutrient-dense foods to the American diet. It favours minimally processed foods including traditional fats such as cod liver oil, lard and tallow, raw dairy, lacto-fermented foods and bone stocks; recommends soaking or souring grains to reduce phytic acid; and opposes the lipid hypothesis, soy and vegetarian diets, as Wikipedia describes.[7]

The foundation campaigns for access to raw milk and helped establish the Farm-to-Consumer Legal Defense Fund in July 2007.[7] The FDA and CDC disagree with its raw-milk health claims, with FDA's John Sheehan quoted by Wikipedia as calling them 'false, devoid of scientific support, and misleading to consumers'.[7] Critics including Quackwatch, Science-Based Medicine's Harriet Hall (2015) and Joel Fuhrman have disputed its dietary positions, a 2007 ScienceBlogs piece used the term 'crank magnetism', and its journal Wise Traditions published pieces in 2022 questioning COVID-19 science, per Wikipedia.[7] The Price-Pottenger Nutrition Foundation, founded in 1952, separately maintains Price's archive.[1]

sections.h: Fat-soluble vitamins and the claimed mechanism
paras: Followers describe the pairing as a way to supply vitamins A, D and K2 together, which they associate with bone and tooth formation. Vitamin K2 (menaquinone) occurs mainly in animal products and fermented foods; butter contains about 15 micrograms per 100 g as MK-4, and hard cheeses, natto, egg yolk and goose liver pate are other sources [8]. K2 is a cofactor for an enzyme that activates Gla proteins, including osteocalcin, which plays an essential role in forming bone mineral [8].

Wikipedia's vitamin K2 article reports that clinical evidence for benefits to bone beyond those of vitamin K1 is inconclusive, though laboratory studies suggest effects K1 does not show; it does not discuss teeth, and it cites a Weston A. Price Foundation article about vitamin K2 for a food-content claim [8].

In the 1920s and 1930s Price also supported the focal infection theory, which led to many tooth extractions; researchers questioned his methods by the 1930s and the theory moved to the margins of dentistry by the 1950s.[1] A 1981 critique by William T. Jarvis in Nutrition Today argued Price's work reflected a 'myth of the healthy savage' and overlooked alternative explanations such as malnutrition.[1] The Weston A. Price Foundation has published a rebuttal to critics.[1]

The reception of the 1939 book has been split along these lines: Hooton and the Canadian Medical Association Journal praised it; Warren T. Vaughan in Scientific Monthly (1940) said some conclusions went far beyond the evidence; and Isaac H. Jones and colleagues in The Laryngoscope (1950) called Price 'The Charles Darwin of Nutrition'.[1] Gunnar Hasselgren's 1994 review of George Meinig's book reviving Price's work argued that Price's research had not been suppressed.[1] Stephen Barrett of Quackwatch dismissed the research as superficial; Wikipedia also reports a cited source stating Price's death certificate listed malnutrition as primary cause of death, with senility contributing.[1]

The Weston A. Price Foundation is a US nonprofit based in Washington, D.C., co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon Morell and Mary G. Enig. Its stated mission is restoring nutrient-dense foods to the American diet through education, research and activism; it promotes minimally processed foods including traditional fats such as cod liver oil, lard and tallow, raw dairy, lacto-fermented foods and bone stocks [7]. It reported about 13,000 members in 2010 and says funding comes from dues, donations and small-company sponsors [7].

The foundation lobbies on dietary guidelines and raw milk access and helped establish the Farm-to-Consumer Legal Defense Fund in 2007. The US FDA has criticised the group's raw-milk health claims, and critics including Quackwatch and Science-Based Medicine have disputed its positions [7].

Cod liver oil is a concentrated source of preformed vitamin A. Wikipedia's hypervitaminosis A article, citing USDA data, says a tablespoon of cod liver oil contains about 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A, above the tolerable upper intake level for every age group listed; adult upper levels are given as 3,000 micrograms per day [9]. Chronic excess is associated with headache, dry or cracked lips, hair loss, peeling skin, bone pain, raised intracranial pressure, hypercalcemia and liver damage [9].

Laboratory work cited in the same article suggests retinoic acid suppresses bone-forming cells and promotes bone resorption, and a review titled 'Is vitamin A consumption a risk factor for osteoporotic fracture?' is among its references [9]. The article notes that possible pregnancy calls for close monitoring and limiting vitamin A intake [9].

Wikipedia's cod liver oil article says a single tablespoon contains about 136 percent of the adult upper limit for vitamin A and that a teaspoon a day exceeds the upper limit for children aged 1 to 8; it also says cod liver oil may benefit secondary prevention after a heart attack through its omega-3 content, and that observational work has correlated daily use with lower rates of severe depression, which does not establish cause.[3]

On looksmax.org, a thread praising Price's book argues that traditional diets produce well-developed faces and teeth across generations, while another thread revisits Price's 1930s palatal expansion case reports and discusses mechanisms for facial and systemic growth.[4][5] A T Nation thread on organ meats likewise cites Price's observations of broad faces and straight teeth among Native Americans eating ancestral diets.[6]

No studies found of fermented cod liver oil combined with high-vitamin butter oil. Related research on butter oil fractions and milk fat has looked at blood lipids and chemistry rather than dental or facial outcomes.[2] Studies of ordinary cod liver oil are covered in the separate cod liver oil article.

lore.intro: Within Weston Price-aligned diet communities and on looksmax.org, the pairing and Price's book are discussed as a route to traditional-food nutrition for teeth and facial development.[1][4][5]

claims.claim: Traditional diets rich in animal fats protect teeth and facial structure.
claims.believers: Proponents of Price's work say he found dental decay rare and well-developed jaws common in groups eating traditional foods, and attribute this to fat-soluble vitamins.[1]
claims.experts: Critics such as William T. Jarvis argued the observations overlooked alternative explanations including malnutrition, and Stephen Barrett said Price ignored life expectancy and infant mortality in the groups studied.[1]

claims.claim: Modern processed food, not genetics, underlies narrow faces and crooked teeth
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says Price's photographs of siblings on traditional versus modern diets show the physical effect of new food products, and that populations on ancestral diets had perfect teeth and little disease.[4]
claims.experts: Critics argued Price's observations overlooked alternative explanations such as malnutrition, and Stephen Barrett said he ignored life expectancy and infant mortality.[1]

claims.claim: Price's palatal expansion cases show jaw widening can improve health and development
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread describes a 1930s case of a teenager with Down syndrome who reportedly gained cognitive, growth and breathing improvements after palatal expansion.[5]
claims.experts: A single historical case report is the basis cited; no controlled studies of these systemic claims have been reported.[5]

claims.claim: Cod liver oil supplies vitamins A and D that support bone and tooth development
claims.believers: Followers describe the oils as supplying fat-soluble vitamins thought to support teeth and bones.[1]
claims.experts: Cod liver oil is a recognised source of vitamins A and D and was used against rickets, though excess vitamin A can accumulate to harmful levels.[3]

claims.claim: Butter oil supplies an 'activator' (vitamin K2) that directs minerals into teeth and bones
claims.believers: Weston Price proponents say butter from grass-fed cows holds a fat-soluble factor that vitamin K2 helps explain, and treat high-vitamin butter oil as a concentrated source of it.
claims.experts: K2 is a cofactor for activating osteocalcin and other Gla proteins; evidence that K2 benefits bone beyond K1 is described as inconclusive, and the Wikipedia article does not address teeth [8].

claims.claim: Fermented cod liver oil is a safe daily source of vitamin A
claims.believers: Followers describe it as a traditional vitamin source and use it for bones and skin.
claims.experts: A tablespoon of cod liver oil exceeds adult upper limits for vitamin A according to USDA figures cited by Wikipedia, and chronic excess is linked with liver damage and bone effects [9][3].

claims.claim: The Weston A. Price Foundation's diet is an evidence-based revival of ancestral nutrition.
claims.believers: Members describe it as restoring traditional foods that protected earlier generations from dental decay and chronic disease.[7]
claims.experts: The FDA and CDC dispute its raw-milk claims, and critics at Quackwatch and Science-Based Medicine describe its positions as questionable; the foundation has published a rebuttal to critics.[1][7]

card.summary: A Weston A. Price Foundation supplement pairing of fermented cod liver oil and butter oil; no clinical studies found.
card.note: Cod liver oil is high in preformed vitamin A, and vitamin A toxicity thresholds apply.

quick.overview:
This is a supplement pairing promoted by followers of dentist Weston A. Price, combining fermented cod liver oil with high-vitamin butter oil as a source of fat-soluble vitamins.
Price's 1939 work on traditional diets drew both praise and criticism from reviewers, and no clinical trials of the combination were found.
quick.mechanism: Followers describe the oils as supplying vitamins A and D and related fat-soluble nutrients thought to support teeth and bone structure. Studies testing that for appearance were not found.
quick.risks: No studies of this specific pairing were found. Cod liver oil is a concentrated source of preformed vitamin A, for which the US upper intake for adults is 3,000 micrograms per day.

chain: Take fermented cod liver oil and high-vitamin butter oil
Supply vitamins A, D and related fat-soluble nutrients
Claimed: better tooth, jaw and bone development
angle.text: Followers take the pairing as a concentrated source of fat-soluble vitamins, following Price's view that traditional nutrient-dense diets produced wide dental arches, straight teeth and strong facial structure. It is also used by adults who want skin and bone support.
